## Assistant

**Yes. Every published planning revision writes a complete snapshot**, including unchanged nodes and relations.

The [storage code](C:/Users/vince/Documents/GitHub/Btr/TheBroccoli/Systems/Depth4/HarnessApp/planning-store.ts:200) writes:

- One JSON file per node.
- One JSON file per relation.
- Metadata containing the accumulated events and operation receipts.

These are separate files—not changes relative to the previous revision, and not shared through hard links.

So **renaming one task rewrites the entire planning graph into another revision folder**. That rollback folder contains **617 revision folders**, explaining how it accumulated over a million entries.

## Assistant

Yes. **We should establish the constraints and their owners before choosing the workflow.** My questions were getting ahead of that.

On your Git question: **some operations work with uncommitted changes; staging is not a general prerequisite or protection.**

- **Fetch** normally downloads history and updates remote-tracking references without changing your working files. We can inspect incoming entry files before pulling; observing incoming changes and integrating them are separate capabilities. [Git fetch](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-fetch), [Git show](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-show).
- **A merge-based pull** can preserve non-overlapping uncommitted edits, but stops when it would overwrite them. Staged changes generally prevent merging too. Automatically stashing and restoring changes can itself introduce conflicts. [Git merge](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-merge#_pre_merge_checks), [Git pull](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-pull).
- **Selected files can be committed independently**, leaving unrelated changes—including staged ones—out of that commit. Our requirement to commit entries without committing unrelated code is therefore achievable. [Git commit](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-commit).
- **A worktree is another checkout of the repository**, with its own working files and staging area, but shared history and branch references. Git normally prevents checking out the same branch in two worktrees simultaneously. [Git worktree](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-worktree).

That gives us this initial constraint inventory:

| Constraint | Consequence for our design |
| --- | --- |
| Unsaved app edits, saved files, staged changes and commits are different states. | A clean Git status does not prove there is no pending work in Broccoli. |
| Entities and relations are ordinary tracked files. | Different worktrees can contain different versions of the same entity. We must distinguish those versions when presenting or editing them. |
| Agents, users and persistence can all write files. | Checkout-changing operations need coordination with those writers. Merely serializing Git commands would not cover the whole problem. |
| A normal pull integrates branch history. | Receiving only selected entry changes is a separate requirement to investigate, not something ordinary pull provides. |
| A buildspace spans independent repositories. | Coordinating their updates must account for partial success; we cannot assume one Git transaction covers them all. |
| External tools remain usable without Broccoli. | Coordination inside Broccoli cannot guarantee control over every external writer; detecting changes and conflicts remains necessary. |

To avoid dependency leakage, **my proposed responsibility allocation** is:

- **GitContributor:** repository/worktree state and Git operations.
- **Decentralized persistence contributor:** configured entity/relation files, synchronization, conflict resolution and its Git integration.
- **RelationalEngine:** selection, observation and invariant primitives used by persistence.
- **The owner of buildspaces and agent execution:** coordinate work across repositories and active agents through those contracts. Agent scheduling policy belongs here.

The first consequence worth discussing is that **a worktree isolates the task files as well as the code**.

**When an agent works in another branch/worktree, do you expect its task progress to appear immediately on your current Activity board, before its work is merged?** That expectation will help us evaluate feasible arrangements against these constraints.

## Assistant

Agreed on the dependency direction: **the agent-work contributor uses system-engineering and buildspace capabilities. Buildspaces remain functional without agentic work.** I’ve recorded that correction.

You’ve also established a concrete requirement: **the Activity board must let you manage and monitor work without switching into each agent’s branch or worktree.** We can evaluate possible arrangements against that requirement without deciding the entire architecture now.

One candidate workflow is:

| Step | Proposed behavior |
| --- | --- |
| You queue a task | The task remains managed in the repository/worktree context where you queued it. |
| An agent starts | The agent contributor creates or selects code worktrees for the required repositories, retaining a reference to that original task. |
| Work progresses or needs attention | The agent contributor requests task updates through system engineering’s operations. Your existing board shows progress and waiting states. Code edits happen in the assigned worktrees. |
| Work becomes ready for review | Results link back to the task. Integrating the code is a separate operation; monitoring did not require merging it first. |

**The central proposal is that the task’s management context and the code’s working context can differ.** Each still has an explicit owner and destination for writes. Persistence handles their configured files; the agent contributor owns the orchestration connecting them.

This is a working hypothesis, with three gaps to investigate before accepting it:

- How we identify the intended task version when the same entity exists in several worktrees.
- How we prevent duplicate execution when several agents observe a queued task.
- How we coordinate task writes and Git operations in the original context, including branch changes or its closure.

Those are concrete constraints I can investigate and bring back as a proposed workflow with limitations. **You shouldn’t have to invent the technical solution to tell me whether the resulting experience fits.**
